what_its_for: This medicine is a solution made from donated human blood that contains antibodies — proteins that help your body fight infections and certain diseases. It is used to boost your immune system if your body does not make enough antibodies on its own (a condition called primary immunodeficiency), to treat certain autoimmune conditions like immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) or Guillain-Barré syndrome, and to help prevent serious infections in people with weakened immune systems.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as an infusion (drip) directly into a vein (intravenously, or IV) or under the skin (subcutaneously), depending on your specific product and doctor's instructions. It is almost always given by a nurse or healthcare provider in a clinic, hospital, or sometimes at home with proper training. Never try to give yourself this infusion without thorough training from your healthcare team. The infusion is given slowly — it may take 2 to 6 hours or longer. You will be monitored during and after the infusion for any reactions.
dosing: Your dose is carefully calculated by your doctor based on your body weight (in kilograms), the condition being treated, and how well your immune system is responding. Doses and how often you receive them vary widely — some people receive infusions every 3 to 4 weeks (monthly), while others may receive smaller doses weekly or more frequently. Always follow your doctor's exact dosing schedule. Do not change your dose or schedule without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a scheduled infusion appointment, contact your doctor or infusion nurse as soon as possible to reschedule. Do not try to double up on doses to make up for a missed one. Missing doses can leave your immune system unprotected, so it is important to stay on schedule as much as possible.
storage: Store unopened vials or bottles in the refrigerator between 2°C and 8°C (36°F and 46°F). Do not freeze. Keep the medicine away from direct light. Some products may be stored at room temperature for a limited time — check the specific instructions on your product's label or ask your pharmacist. Once the vial has been opened or the infusion has been prepared, it must be used right away or within the time frame stated on the product label. Do not use if the solution looks cloudy, has particles floating in it, or if the expiry date has passed.
what_to_avoid: Avoid receiving live vaccines (such as the MMR or chickenpox vaccine) for at least 3 months after receiving this medicine, as it may make those vaccines less effective — always let your doctor or pharmacist know you are on this treatment before any vaccinations. Avoid activities that could cause injury right after your infusion if you feel dizzy or unwell. Let all your healthcare providers know you are receiving immune globulin, as it may affect certain blood test results.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or seek emergency help immediately if you experience: severe headache, stiff neck, sensitivity to light, or fever (these may be signs of a rare but serious condition called aseptic meningitis); sudden back or leg pain, blood in your urine, decreased urination, or swelling (possible kidney problems); chest pain, difficulty breathing, or a bluish color to your lips or fingertips (possible lung or heart problems); blood clots, which can cause leg pain or swelling, arm pain, sudden vision changes, confusion, or one-sided weakness; dark or cola-colored urine, unusual tiredness, or yellowing of the skin or eyes (possible signs of red blood cell breakdown); hives, itching, rash, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing during or after the infusion (possible allergic reaction). Also call your doctor if you develop a fever, chills, or signs of infection after your infusion.
when_it_works: For immune deficiency conditions, you may start to notice fewer and less severe infections within a few weeks to months of starting treatment as your antibody levels build up. For conditions like ITP, platelet counts may improve within a few days to a week after the infusion. Full benefits may take longer depending on your condition, so keep all follow-up appointments so your doctor can check your progress with blood tests.
special_populations: Elderly patients (65 and older): Use with extra caution because there is a higher risk of blood clots and kidney problems. Your doctor will use the lowest effective dose and monitor you closely. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: This medicine may be used during pregnancy when the benefits outweigh the risks; talk to your doctor. It may pass into breast milk, but this is generally considered safe. Kidney problems: Tell your doctor if you have any kidney disease, as this medicine — especially the maltose-containing formulations — may worsen kidney function. Your doctor will choose a formulation and dose carefully. Diabetes: Important — some glucose monitors may give false high readings when you are receiving IgG products containing maltose or hippurate. Use a glucose-specific testing method (not maltose-reactive test strips) to avoid incorrect insulin dosing. Always inform your diabetes care team that you are on this medicine. IgA deficiency: If you have a known IgA deficiency with antibodies against IgA, you are at higher risk of a severe allergic reaction. Tell your doctor before starting treatment.
